description: Proving Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2025.

talks.title: Broke but Breached: Secret Scanning at Scale on a Student Budget
talks.teaser: Shows how cheap cloud credits and Kubernetes were used to scan VS Code extensions for leaked credentials.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a recent graduate, opened with how leaked credentials have fed real breaches and why they are preventable with pipeline checks. The research targeted Visual Studio Code extensions from the marketplace, many of which ship with embedded environment variables, and the number of new extensions grew sharply through AI-assisted coding. Early runs used friends' Azure accounts, but CPU-heavy scanning crashed some VMs, so the pipeline moved to a managed DigitalOcean Kubernetes cluster that used free student credits.

The pipeline had three stages: gathering extension links from the marketplace sitemap, scanning packages with TruffleHog, and normalizing results. Scanner pods ran on every node, with a Go orchestrator, PostgreSQL storage and an SQS queue, reaching roughly 100 extensions per minute. Verified findings included cloud and AI service keys, GitHub and npm tokens, and Hugging Face tokens; one npm token remained valid years after its extension was last updated. Blocked IP addresses were handled by rotating them through a queue with a cooldown timer, and the whole effort cost under $15.

Trends shifted from blockchain API keys around 2022 to AI service keys by 2025. The takeaway is that attackers could run similar work at far larger scale, so developers should scan before commits and in pipelines, rotate exposed secrets, and enable logging with alerts for unusual credential use. Future plans include the JetBrains and Open VSX marketplaces.

talks.title: Take all my money - penetrating ATMs
talks.teaser: Examines how ATMs can be penetrated, with the theft of their cash as the central goal.

talks.title: Malicious Packages - they're gonna get ya!
talks.teaser: Explains how malicious packages reach developer machines and why scanners and SCA tools alone cannot stop them.
talks.summary:
The talk covers malicious dependencies, which are built to cause harm and often act the first time they run, unlike vulnerable ones. They live in public registries such as npm and PyPI and often target developer machines, where credentials and API keys sit in environment variables. Attackers hide code through encoding, obfuscation, blending into useful code, or nesting it as a subdependency. Vendor counts show rapid growth, though that vendor sells a product in this space.

Attacks are grouped by when they strike. Typosquatting is the most common tactic when adding a dependency, and slopsquatting exploits package names that AI assistants invent. For packages already in use, dependency confusion can substitute a public package for an internal one, and hijacking happens through expired domains or stolen credentials. Phishing also works: a popular linter was compromised after a maintainer took a phishing bait, and a Linux compression utility was backdoored after an attacker pressured its sole maintainer over three years.

Defenses include developer awareness, package name and history checks, and code scanning, though each has gaps. Software composition analysis tools mainly flag known vulnerabilities, often run too late to stop a malicious install, and may skip development dependencies. Endpoint detection can catch known behavior, private registries offer control if configured carefully, and newer services block packages flagged as malicious. The main takeaway is that no single control is enough, so teams should layer several defenses.

talks.title: Let's Go Shopping: Third-Party Vendors and CyberRisk
talks.teaser: Uses grocery shopping analogies to explain third-party vendor risk, criticality, inherent and residual risk for business decisions.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents third-party risk management as a balance between the value a purchase offers and the impact and likelihood of harm it could cause. Rather than opening with security jargon, the talk asks listeners to reason the way they already do in a grocery store, weighing what they truly need against what they merely want and what they already have on hand.

Walking through a supermarket, the session places deli food, cleaning supplies, raw meat, produce and flowers on an impact-versus-probability grid. Controls such as expiration dates, government rules, store policies and food handling courses then lower the residual risk that remains. The talk also shows that risk moves over time: a Valentine's Day shortage or the 2020 supply disruption changed how the same items felt. Business cases follow, including a 2014 retail breach that entered through an HVAC vendor, and a 2024 incident at a well-known security vendor that showed how widely trusted software was embedded.

For practitioners, the closing advice is to have colleagues ask whether a tool is needed, what data or systems it touches, how much the organization would lose if it failed, and whether the business owner would accept that outcome. Certifications are described as a useful starting point for due diligence rather than a final answer, and build-versus-buy decisions depend on available resources. The speaker noted that the operational side of vendor evaluation is a separate conversation for analysts.

talks.title: Boost Your Career: Get Practical InfoSec Experience in Your Community
talks.teaser: Explains how volunteering at a community computer lab builds hands-on security skills and supports career growth.
talks.summary:
Ashley Cihak, president of a Northern Nevada Lions Club chapter, makes the case that volunteer work can build real security and technical skills. The club's computers-for-kids program gives low-income students from kindergarten through twelfth grade refurbished laptops and desktops, and a monthly two-hour lab walks them through account setup, strong passphrases, Linux and open-source tools, and basic online safety. Parental controls are included for families. The club also trains its own volunteers, including lawyers, accountants and people new to the field, to load and standardize Linux systems.

The middle of the talk covers what volunteers gain beyond technical work. Running labs and donation drives builds project management, inventory tracking, troubleshooting, leadership and people-handling skills, and volunteer hours can count toward continuing professional education. The speaker cited survey figures on skills-based hiring and on volunteering strengthening professional skill sets. The club also partnered with the Center for Internet Security to test a CIS-compliant desktop image with its students, giving volunteers exposure to hardening work.

The closing section shares outcomes: a former foster student who later ran a tech company and hired young people leaving foster care, a seven-year-old who began keeping her mother's bookkeeping in a spreadsheet, and a volunteer who gained command-line experience and was hired by a local data center. Listeners are encouraged to join a local Lions Club, start a similar program, or teach basic skills at libraries, YMCAs and community centers.

talks.title: Unawakened Wakeup: A Novel PHP Object Injection Technique to Bypass __wakeup()
talks.teaser: Shows how a class-instantiation weakness can bypass PHP __wakeup() guards inside deserialization gadget chains.
talks.summary:
PHP object injection happens when untrusted input reaches unserialize(), letting an attacker shape the objects that get restored. Developers often add __wakeup() methods to block this, but such guards are not reliable, and some known bypasses are losing effect in newer PHP releases.

The talk focuses on a class-instantiation weakness: when an application builds a class from a user-supplied name without validation, the object is created without __wakeup() ever running. A class that does this can act as a link in a property-oriented gadget chain, so an attacker can reach a protected gadget indirectly. To show this is practical, the speaker revives an older Guzzle chain that a wakeup guard had broken, using gadgets from Flow, a PHP web framework, along with Doctrine. A live demonstration then runs a command against a test application, though only part of the demo was shown.

For defenders, the takeaway is to avoid native PHP serialization for untrusted data, move to JSON, or sign serialized payloads with an HMAC as the PHP manual recommends. For testers, dynamic instantiation points are worth searching for during code review, because they can widen what a deserialization bug is able to reach.

talks.title: RAGnarok: Assisting Your Threat Hunting with Local LLM
talks.teaser: Shows how a quantized local LLM with retrieval and agents drafts Sigma detection rules offline on a CPU.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical problem: threat hunting involves many repetitive steps, and cloud-hosted language models raise concerns because network configuration and other sensitive data should not leave the organization. The speaker presents Ragnarok, a tool that turns threat intelligence about an attack technique into a Sigma detection rule using a model that runs on a CPU-only machine.

The design combines three ideas. A quantized model reduces the computing resources needed, retrieval-augmented generation pulls reference material such as Sigma guidance and Microsoft documentation from a vector store, and a multi-agent workflow divides the work. For Active Directory techniques, one agent gathers configuration data from an AD mapping tool, stores it in a graph database and queries it for relevant findings. A demo walked through loading and crawling reference documents, generating a rule, converting it to SPL and testing it in a demo environment, with manual review still required.

The lessons were practical. Filtering the MITRE ATT&CK detection text before generation mattered because irrelevant content produced poor rules. Token limits can halt long multi-agent runs, so summarizing context helped. Windows event log formats vary by event ID, which led to a dedicated lookup tool. Chunking by meaningful units such as paragraphs strongly affected accuracy, and large document sets increased indexing time and disk use. The speaker concluded that local models suit sensitive environments, but each technique carries tradeoffs.

talks.title: SIGMA, one rule to find them all
talks.teaser: Shows how Sigma's platform-neutral rule format lets defenders write detections once and translate them to many SIEMs and EDRs.
talks.summary:
Rain Baker opens with background on Sigma, a community detection format created by Florian Roth and Thomas Patzke. Rules are written in YAML and are meant to be platform agnostic, working on log data much as YARA works on files. The talk walks through the required parts of a rule: a title, a log source defined by category, product and service, a detection section built from named selections, and a condition that combines them with boolean logic. Modifiers such as contains and filters that cut noise are also covered.

The middle of the talk shows example rules built from strings pulled from malware samples in customer environments and from sandbox detonations. Examples include a PowerShell download rule, an encoded PowerShell rule keyed on a hidden window and an Explorer parent process, and a rule for a ClickFix-style lure that prints text to the command line. A web converter built on pySigma pipelines was demonstrated, turning a rule into queries for backends such as Splunk, CrowdStrike and Carbon Black.

The closing section covers practical limits. Translation is not always clean, since Splunk field names vary by environment and a generic conversion can miss events without a custom pipeline. Rule ideas come from the team's own telemetry, fresh threat intelligence, customer requests and community repositories. The speaker's team tracks rules in Jira, vets them through weekly sprints with hunters, and then either promotes them to detections or uses them as leads for hunts.

talks.title: Harnessing AI and Post-Quantum Cryptography for Cybersecurity in the Quantum Era
talks.teaser: Shows how AI-based anomaly detection and post-quantum cryptography can counter harvest-now, decrypt-later data theft.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a state-linked group that quietly moves sensitive data out through web traffic. Quantum computers would eventually break RSA and ECC through Shor's algorithm and weaken symmetric keys through Grover's, though AES-256 remains considered post-quantum safe. Meanwhile, harvest-now, decrypt-later campaigns already collect long-lived data such as intellectual property and government secrets for future decryption.

Conventional tools such as IDS, IPS, DLP and next-generation firewalls catch known threats but miss zero-days and stealthy intruders. AI can add behavioral analytics, adaptive firewall tuning and predictive threat modeling. The speaker compared isolation forests, autoencoders and variational autoencoders on a network intrusion dataset with about 18 features, and autoencoders performed best on accuracy, precision and recall. Precision keeps false alarms manageable, while high recall is key for catching slow, silent exfiltration.

The transition plan starts with a cryptographic inventory covering algorithms, key sizes, rotation practices and how long protected data must stay confidential. Teams should build crypto agility through modular libraries, consider hybrid schemes during migration, and move toward the NIST-standardized ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA algorithms while following CNSA and NIST guidance. The closing message was that these changes are continuous rather than one-time, so planning should begin now.

talks.title: I Didn’t Register for This: What’s Really in Google’s Artifact Registry?
talks.teaser: Shows how scanning Google-owned container images in Artifact Registry exposed many vulnerabilities and leaked secrets.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a cloud vulnerability researcher who, while examining Google Cloud Composer, found a Kubernetes configuration pulling an image from Artifact Registry. Image tags tied it to Google's organization ID, suggesting Google had published it for production use. A missing list permission blocked browsing the project, but the legacy gcr.io domain exposed more Google-uploaded images.

Scanning the gathered images covered over 3,000 images from 32 repositories, sorted into three groups: third-party marketplace images, Google's base images, and images Google runs in its own production. The results showed about 1.7 million vulnerability findings, roughly 350,000 unique CVEs, and many critical issues, including Log4Shell, Zerologon and Spring4Shell. Nearly 3,000 secrets appeared, all in marketplace images, among them cloud credentials, API keys and hard-coded administrator logins. Google said it had checked the production images but could not judge exploitability for marketplace ones.

The speaker urged users never to assume trust based on the publisher, to scan images for secrets and vulnerabilities, to keep marketplace images patched, and to audit what actually runs in their environments. The talk closes by questioning the shared responsibility model, since marketplace documentation puts vulnerability-free requirements on vendors while the review process involves Google scanning.

talks.title: The Perfect BLEnd: Reverse engineering a bluetooth controlled blender for better smoothies
talks.teaser: Shows how a Bluetooth blender's protocol was reverse engineered to build custom blend profiles without the vendor app.
talks.summary:
The speaker's smart blender could only be controlled through a phone app. That app was last updated years earlier and no longer found the device on a newer phone, and there was no way to start the blender from a computer or to save custom blend timings. The talk sets out to learn how the phone and the blender communicate over Bluetooth Low Energy, where the blender acts as a peripheral exposing custom services and characteristics.

The first attempts used a dedicated BLE sniffer, which needed close range and often missed the connection. The approach moved to capturing the Bluetooth host controller traffic from an iPhone, then filtering for write requests from the phone to the blender. Comparing the written bytes against known blend durations suggested that one byte tracks run time and that the paired on and off steps form a sequence, with the speed stored in part of another byte. Decompiling the Android app's native library and reading its SQLite preset database helped confirm the layout. Some characteristics, such as those tied to a connected scale, were traced to publicly available code from other projects.

The speaker used a generated web Bluetooth app to send a custom three-step profile to the blender, and the demo ran it as written. The takeaways were that a vendor app being discontinued can strand working hardware, and that the blender's protocol had no pairing or authentication, so range was the only practical limit on who could send commands. A physical lid interlock still had to be engaged before the motor would run.

talks.title: Community Defense in Depth: Teaching digital security and privacy practices for the public good
talks.teaser: Shows how journalists, activists and other vulnerable people can threat model their devices, data and communities.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a news story about a woman who travelled out of state for an abortion, where a family's request for a wellness check showed how widely available license plate reader data can reveal a person's movements. The speaker presents threat modeling as harm reduction, using the STRIDE framework, and stresses that race, age, income and disability all change a person's threat model.

Two personas anchor the middle of the session. A freelance journalist returning through a border zone faces device searches, so the advice covers unique passwords for each app, backing up notes, powering off devices before inspection, uploading files to encrypted storage before travel, and collecting less sensitive data in the first place. A young activist distributing mutual aid at protests faces facial recognition unlocks, payment fraud and doxxing, so the suggestions include using a passcode rather than biometrics, moving sensitive chats to encrypted messaging, hiding location in photos, verifying callers before sending money, and asking trusted friends to manage accounts during harassment. Street cameras, cell site simulators and a military surveillance drone are described as examples of tools that can track people on the ground.

The talk closes by asking attendees to make one privacy change today, help a friend or neighbour with their own threat model, and consider who in their community would benefit most from the same exercise. The main lesson for practitioners is to start from the attacker's point of view and apply least privilege to every tool and dataset.

talks.title: Innovative, Shiny, and Vulnerable: Four Ways to Exploit Modern SaaS Data Platforms
talks.teaser: Walks through four ways attackers can exploit SaaS data platforms, from access control flaws to abusing serverless scaling.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at SaaS data platforms that ingest large volumes of customer and proprietary data and hold privileged credentials for third-party systems. Because these products are publicly exposed and tightly tied to business processes, weaknesses in them create supply chain and third-party risk. The speaker uses a demonstration platform to walk through the attack paths.

The first avenue is control plane access control, where broken object-level authorization lets users reach other workspaces or tenants, and predictable identifiers make enumeration easy. The second is abusing the platform's job feature, which runs user-supplied scripts. Command execution on the runner exposed the container's startup configuration, including an overprivileged service account key that could read secrets for other organizations. Instance metadata then yielded a cloud role able to list a storage bucket of execution logs containing personal data.

The fourth vector is serverless abuse: a single request set up an infinite loop through a streaming API and a Lambda function, pushing over ten million events in about two minutes and exhausting a free tier. Attackers could drive costs, cause denial of service against third parties, or trigger provider intervention. The takeaways are to test authorization on every endpoint, keep runner secrets scoped to the job, restrict cloud roles to the tenant, and threat model cost abuse in serverless designs.

talks.title: Security Theater, Now Playing: When Security Is a Sideshow Instead of a Strategy
talks.teaser: Explains how security teams can move from compliance-heavy gatekeeping to becoming trusted partners in product development.
talks.summary:
Mia Kralowetz, who moved into full-time security about five years ago after contract penetration testing and a finance background, describes a pattern common at startups: security gets built in only after a company reaches product-market fit. She recounts a payments-app pivot where her team brought leadership a stack of lengthy risk assessments and threat models. Executives wanted a short summary, the report went largely unread, the feature launched anyway, and security lost its seat in important meetings and some of its budget.

The middle of the talk covers how her team rebuilt trust. They moved from being a department of no to a department of how, joined roadmap discussions early, and timed their feedback so it landed before designs were locked. For less mature engineering teams they published sample repositories and reference architecture, and they used a risk-based multiplier in prioritization so security appeared in product planning. They framed risk in business terms that executives could weigh, and they routed checks through CI/CD so developers saw findings in the tools they already used.

She closes with questions security staff can ask about any new feature: what it does, what it should do, what value it adds, how long the review can take, how attackers could abuse it, and what could go wrong. The practical takeaway is to learn the product well, earn trust rather than assume it, and act as a thought partner. In the Q&A she added that business-defined thresholds make labels like high and medium meaningful.

talks.title: Shorts Begone: Modding YouTube on iOS (without jailbreaking)
talks.teaser: Shows how to modify the iOS YouTube app to hide Shorts, using sideloading and runtime hooks instead of a jailbreak.
talks.summary:
The speaker starts from a personal annoyance: the Shorts feed in the YouTube app keeps pulling viewers into long, unplanned sessions. Inspired by an earlier project that modded TikTok, the goal was to change a stock iOS app on a phone that cannot be jailbroken. The talk gives a short history of iOS modding, from the restricted early iPhone years through the period of popular tweaks, and explains why that scene has slowed.

The method has three stages: obtain a decrypted app package, sideload it with an in-app debugging overlay, then inspect the view hierarchy to find the Shorts tab and its playback screen. The speaker explains method swizzling, first hiding the tab with a runtime hook and then simulating a back action whenever a Short starts playing. Other tools covered include Flex for live inspection, Theos and Logos to reduce boilerplate, and running an iOS app on an Apple silicon Mac so LLDB can attach to it. A demo also showed an AI agent driving LLDB to locate and change UI elements, with uneven results.

The main takeaways are that app packages are signed and encrypted, but decrypted copies can be sideloaded under free or paid developer accounts, with re-signing needed on a weekly or yearly cycle. Hooks break when the app updates, so a fixed version is the practical target. The Q&A covered how long a decrypted build stays usable and whether community tooling can keep pace with YouTube changes.

talks.title: Azazel System: Tactical Delaying Action via the Cyber-Scapegoat Gateway
talks.teaser: Describes Azazel, a system that uses a cyber-scapegoat gateway to delay attackers tactically.

talks.title: Yes, We Still Exist in the Era of AI!!!
talks.teaser: Shows how AI features in desktop applications widen old attack surfaces, with prompt injection and file-format fuzzing demos.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that desktop applications remain a target as AI features such as local assistants, predictive interfaces and on-device models spread into engineering, creative and finance software. The speaker reviews familiar desktop weaknesses: memory corruption in legacy native code, privilege escalation through services running as system, world-writable folders and hardcoded credentials.

Demonstrations used a deliberately vulnerable assistant built for the talk. Crafted prompts overrode the system prompt and led the assistant to describe attack methods and reveal its own backend API keys, which were already revoked. A tampered local model returned poor security advice such as weak default passwords. The speaker then argued that AI-generated or malformed files could reach fragile parsers, turning model output into a memory corruption path.

Recommendations centered on fuzzing AI inputs alongside file formats and protocols, building AI-specific threat models with abuse case testing, validating inputs and outputs, and signing and verifying model files. Limiting privileges for AI features and plugin or macro integrations, and defining trust boundaries between AI and legacy components, were also highlighted. In the Q&A, the speaker said local apps are harder to protect than cloud services because the software ships to customer machines, so integrity checks and code hardening matter more.

talks.title: Cognitive Agents Delivering Wisdom at Scale
talks.teaser: Shows how LLM-based agents can reconstruct attack timelines and rank SOC alerts by business impact.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the strain on security operations centers: analysts lose much of their day triaging alerts that turn out to be nothing, while alert volumes keep climbing and attackers increasingly use AI. The speaker argues the goal is collaboration between humans and agents, not replacement, and traces detection from isolated alerts to correlated incidents. The next step described is reasoning about why an event happened and how much it matters.

The proposed design is a set of LLM-based agents. An orchestrator runs SOP-style playbooks and holds approval guardrails. An investigator gathers context such as asset ownership and threat intelligence and builds an end-to-end story; one demo assembled a business email compromise from four separate alerts. A prioritizer rates whether that story is a true positive, with a confidence score and recommended actions. A responder can contain threats within permitted limits, a hunter searches for similar activity elsewhere, and a rule-writing agent turns lessons from an incident into new detections. The demos used scrubbed client data in a test environment.

The expected outcomes are less noise, faster containment, and lower analyst burnout. Adoption advice is to start small, target one pain point with a single agent, measure results and iterate. In the questions, the speaker acknowledged that prompt injection from untrusted data is a concern not yet addressed, and that enforcing SOPs from varied sources relies on code-level guardrails. Smaller specialized models were suggested as a way to cut cost.

talks.title: Detect and Respond? Cool Story — or Just Don’t Let the Bad Stuff Start.
talks.teaser: Shows how admission policies and runtime enforcement can stop a Kubernetes container compromise before an attacker gains a foothold.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Kubernetes workloads should be hardened before they run, rather than relying mainly on detection and response afterwards. The presenter uses an analogy about a building where guards, locked doors and access rules prevent problems up front, with cameras serving as a backup. The default Kubernetes setup offers little protection: container images often run as root with package managers installed, and pods and deployments run whatever the container asks for.

To make this concrete, the presenter follows a small Python app with a deliberately planted command-execution flaw. A single request gives an attacker a root shell inside the container, from which they can install scanning tools, read sensitive files and reach the mounted service account token. Kyverno is then introduced as an admission controller that validates deployments before they enter the cluster. A policy in enforce mode rejects pods that do not set a non-root security context, and it returns a readable message to the developer. The presenter notes that mutating the manifest instead can leave the container unable to start.

Next, KubeArmor restricts behaviour at execution time using Linux security modules. Its policies block writes to /tmp, block running the Python binary that would be used for listeners, and block shell access, while the legitimate Flask app keeps working. The presenter acknowledges limits: some workloads genuinely need root, and some normal activity can look suspicious. Runtime observability with eBPF is suggested as a way to watch what gets through. The main takeaway is to validate configuration at admission, restrict what containers can execute, and keep monitoring as a backstop. Node and cluster hardening were left out of scope.
